query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In solidified equiatomic Co‐free FeNiCrMn, the dynamic response across temperature and strain‐rate regimes is primarily controlled by dislocation nucleation at grain boundaries that produces stacking faults. At moderate strain rates and temperatures, thermally activated dislocation glide and stacking fault formation ensure a balance between strength and ductility, while at high strain rates (or lower temperatures) viscous phonon drag impedes dislocation motion, leading to increased yield strength. This interplay of grain-boundary‐mediated nucleation, stacking fault development, and rate-dependent phonon drag governs the observed dynamic behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: Solidified, equiatomic, Co-free FeNiCrMn with a predominantly FCC structure and controlled fine grain size.
generation.intervention: Subject the material to dynamic mechanical loading (tension and compression) under a range of strain rates (from quasi-static to ~10^3 s^-1) and temperatures (e.g., 300 K vs 900 K).
generation.conditions: Tests performed on samples with uniform microstructure (minimal extrinsic defects) and similar grain sizes to isolate the role of grain-boundary mediated dislocation activity.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries serving as nucleation sites for Shockley partial dislocations and the resulting stacking faults.
generation.mechanism: Dynamic loading triggers dislocation nucleation at grain boundaries. At moderate strain rates and temperatures, thermally activated dislocation glide and stacking fault formation facilitate plastic deformation with maintained ductility. Under high strain rates (or lower temperatures), limited time for thermally activated processes together with increased viscous phonon drag enhances dislocation entanglement and yield strength, thereby shifting the dynamic response.
generation.predicted_outcome: At lower strain rates and moderate temperatures the alloy will show moderate increases in yield strength accompanied by sustained ductility through active stacking fault formation. At higher strain rates (or lower temperatures), the material will exhibit a marked increase in yield strength and reduced ductility due to enhanced phonon drag and dislocation entanglement.
generation.baseline: The expected behavior based on conventional single-phase FCC HEAs, which typically do not show such pronounced strain-rate sensitivity when grain-boundary mediated dislocation nucleation is not the dominating mechanism.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to solidified, equiatomic Co-free FeNiCrMn with controlled fine grain microstructures; deviations may occur in samples with significantly different grain sizes, defect densities, or non-equiatomic compositions.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative contributions of thermally activated slip versus phonon drag, and the precise strain rate or temperature thresholds at which the transition occurs, remain to be established experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare Co-free FeNiCrMn samples with uniform, fine grain structures and subject them to dynamic tension and compression tests over a range of strain rates (from 10^-3 s^-1 to 10^3 s^-1) at different temperatures (e.g., 300 K and 900 K). In situ high-resolution imaging (e.g., TEM) or diffraction techniques (e.g., high-speed XRD) should be used to monitor dislocation nucleation, stacking fault formation, and phase changes.
measurements: Stress–strain curves to capture yield strength and ductility variations
Real-time imaging of dislocation nucleation sites and stacking fault evolution
Quantification of dislocation densities and entanglement levels
Assessment of phase fractions (FCC/BCC, etc.) during deformation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experiments do not show a significant correlation between grain-boundary mediated stacking fault formation (or dislocation nucleation) and the observed changes in dynamic strength and ductility with strain rate and temperature, or if an alternative mechanism (e.g., twinning or grain boundary sliding) dominates the plastic deformation response, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The role of GBs in the mechanical deformation of HEA alloys remains poorly understood. Tensile stress-strain diagrams for Cantor alloy bicrystals with [110] and [111] loading axes show that GBs facilitate the nucleation of partial dislocations, which with further deformation grow in the bulk crystal leaving behind stacking faults. This is in agreement with recent experimental findings demonstrating that GBs act as nucleation sites for mechanical nanotwins,. cited_evidence.kind: web:3.1. Deformation Behavior of Ag NWs and CoNiCrFeMn HEA NWs
cited_evidence.text: At 300 K, stress in CoNiCrFeMn HEA NW reaches up to 5.5 GPa at around 5% strain, as shown in Figure 2b during elastic deformation. Multiple partial dislocations nucleate simultaneously at different slip planes across NW as can be seen in Figure 5b. It has been thought that HEAs own the lattice distortion effect which will be amplified under higher temperatures. Therefore, the activation barriers of dislocation nucleation could be lower than those at 77 K, which gives rise to more partial dislocation nucleation at different sites. Subsequently, on further loading, more partial dislocations nucleate and glide through the NW, inducing the deformation twinning and martensitic transformation to the HCP phase. Interestingly, the reorientation mechanism can still exist and contribute to the extended plasticity until the fracture of NW caused by necking as shown in Figure 5b. Overall, the exceptional strength-ductility trade-off of HEA NW at low temperature is a synergistic result of operative mechanisms involving the twinning, phase transformation, and also the re-orientation of the NW cross-section. Compressive yield strength was calculated at 5% strain and plotted on a double-logarithmic scale of flow stress (MPa) versus strain rate (s−1) as shown in Fig. 3c. SRS of two different regimes was obtained from the slope of a linear fit as shown by the dotted lines. The SRS was 0.03 for low strain rates (10–3 s−1–10–1 s−1) while it was about an order of magnitude higher with a value of 0.2 in the high strain rate (102 s−1–103 s−1) regime. At low strain rates, dislocation velocities are small and that leads to negligible effect of phonon drag on dislocation motion. Therefore, flow stress changes at a slower rate with change in strain rate and mostly depends on thermally activated dislocation glide. The SRS value of our alloy is larger compared to other single-phase FCC HEAs reported in literature, such as Al0.1CoCrFeNi and CoCrFeMnNi. The high SRS value at high strain rates may be attributed to two factors: (i) not enough time for thermally activated dislocations to cross the energy barrier and (ii) strong effect of viscous phonon drag on dislocation motion.
